Clinical utility of pre-extubation respiratory sampling

TIM POP study — Final statistical analysis

Author

Alexandre Sitbon

Executive summary

This analysis is based on the final locked TIM POP database, comprising 122 patients with postoperative pneumonia (POP), all of whom underwent pre-extubation respiratory sampling.

NoteKey findings
  • Pre-extubation microbiological yield: 81/122 (66.4%)
  • Broad microbiological concordance: 54/81 (66.7%)
  • Specific concordance excluding oropharyngeal flora: 33/81 (40.7%)
  • Specific concordance in the overall cohort: 33/122 (27.0%)
  • Inadequate empirical antimicrobial therapy: 22/100 (22.0%)
  • Potentially actionable prior microbiology: 8/122 (6.6%)
  • Resistance and empirical inadequacy: OR 10.02 (95% CI 3.13–36.66; P <0.001)

Pre-extubation respiratory microbiology frequently identified microorganisms and showed subsequent organism-specific concordance in a substantial subset of patients. However, prior organism-specific information coincided with subsequent inadequate empirical antimicrobial therapy in only a minority of the overall cohort.

Potential actionability should be interpreted as an upper-bound estimate, because the precise time at which microbiological identification and antimicrobial susceptibility results became available to clinicians is unknown.

Main results

Study population and microbiological yield

The FINAL analytical cohort comprised 122 patients with postoperative pneumonia.

Pre-extubation respiratory sampling was performed in 122/122 (100.0%) patients.

Among these samples:

  • 81 were positive;
  • 41 were negative.

The microbiological yield was therefore 81/122 (66.4%; 95% CI 57.3–74.7%).

Microbiological concordance

At least one microorganism recovered before extubation was subsequently recovered at POP diagnosis in 54/81 (66.7%; 95% CI 55.3–76.8%) positive pre-extubation samples.

Because non-specific oropharyngeal flora may artificially inflate apparent microbiological overlap, the principal organism-specific analysis excluded oropharyngeal flora from both pre-extubation and POP samples.

After this exclusion, specific organism-level concordance was observed in 33/81 (40.7%; 95% CI 29.9–52.2%) positive pre-extubation samples.

This corresponded to 33/122 (27.0%) of the overall cohort.

Microbiological trajectories

Beyond the overall concordance rate, we examined individual microbiological trajectories between positive pre-extubation respiratory samples and subsequent POP microbiology.

The Sankey plot illustrates the relationship between microorganisms identified before extubation and those subsequently recovered at POP diagnosis. Flows are classified according to whether at least one specific microorganism, excluding non-specific oropharyngeal flora, was recovered at both time points.

Among the 81 patients with positive pre-extubation microbiology, at least one microorganism was subsequently recovered at POP diagnosis in 54 (66.7%) patients.

After exclusion of non-specific oropharyngeal flora, specific organism-level concordance remained in 33/81 (40.7%) patients.

The Sankey representation nevertheless demonstrates substantial microbiological turnover between the two sampling periods: a positive pre-extubation respiratory sample did not necessarily identify the specific microorganism subsequently recovered at POP diagnosis.

Importantly, microbiological concordance alone does not establish clinical utility. The subsequent analysis therefore evaluates whether concordant pre-extubation information could potentially have altered empirical antimicrobial selection.

Potential clinical actionability

The clinically relevant subgroup was defined by the combination of:

  1. positive pre-extubation respiratory microbiology;
  2. specific organism-level concordance with subsequent POP;
  3. inadequate empirical antimicrobial therapy at POP diagnosis.

Among the 33 patients with specific microbiological concordance, 8 subsequently received inadequate empirical antimicrobial therapy.

Thus, prior organism-specific microbiological information was potentially relevant to empirical antimicrobial selection in 8/122 (6.6%; 95% CI 2.9–12.5%) of the overall cohort.

WarningInterpretation

The 8/122 estimate represents potential rather than demonstrated clinical actionability.

The FINAL database establishes the date of pre-extubation sampling but does not establish the precise time at which microorganism identification and antimicrobial susceptibility results became available to clinicians.

Empirical antimicrobial adequacy

Empirical antimicrobial adequacy could be assessed in 100/122 patients.

Empirical therapy was:

  • adequate in 78/100 (78.0%);
  • inadequate in 22/100 (22.0%).
Empirical antimicrobial adequacy according to pre-extubation microbiological positivity.
Pre-EOT microbiology n Inadequate therapy
Negative 25 6/25 (24.0%)
Positive 75 16/75 (21.3%)

This comparison is descriptive because pre-extubation microbiological positivity may reflect differences in patient characteristics and respiratory microbial ecology.

Antimicrobial resistance and empirical treatment inadequacy

Resistance phenotype information was interpretable in 110 patients, of whom 32 (29.1%) had at least one reported antimicrobial resistance phenotype.

Empirical antimicrobial inadequacy was substantially more frequent in patients with a reported antimicrobial resistance phenotype.

The unadjusted association between reported antimicrobial resistance and empirical antimicrobial inadequacy corresponded to an OR of 10.02 (95% CI 3.13–36.66; P <0.001).

This association is exploratory and should not be interpreted as evidence of an independent causal effect.

Potentially actionable cases

Eight patients combined specific pre-extubation/POP microbiological concordance with subsequent inadequate empirical antimicrobial therapy.

NoteWhy these cases matter

These patients define the maximum subgroup in which prior organism-specific microbiological information might theoretically have influenced empirical antimicrobial selection.

They do not demonstrate that prior microbiological information was available or acted upon when empirical therapy was prescribed.

Database integrity

The FINAL analytical database contains 122 patients, 125 variables, and 122 unique patient identifiers, with no duplicated patient identifier.

Coding decisions

Pre-extubation sampling

According to the FINAL dictionary:

  • 0 = no respiratory sample;
  • 1 = protected distal sampling;
  • 2 = tracheal aspirate;
  • 3 = sputum sample;
  • 4 = bronchoalveolar lavage.

Absence of sampling is therefore defined by code 0, rather than missingness.

Distribution of pre-extubation sampling codes.
Sampling code n
1 55
2 18
4 49

Binary variables

Some FINAL database cells contain the text value "Autre" in otherwise binary variables.

These values were not recoded as either 0 or 1 and were treated as unavailable for the corresponding analysis.

Antimicrobial resistance coding

According to the FINAL dictionary:

  • 0 = no reported resistance;
  • 1 = ESBL;
  • 2 = carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales;
  • 3 = methicillin resistance;
  • 4 = cephalosporinase;
  • 5 = highly resistant Pseudomonas phenotype.

Codes 1–5 were grouped as any reported antimicrobial resistance for the binary resistance analysis.

Core analytical definitions

Positive pre-extubation microbiology

A pre-extubation respiratory sample was considered positive when at least one microorganism code >0 was recorded in one of the three microorganism fields.

Broad microbiological concordance

Broad concordance was defined as recovery at POP diagnosis of at least one microorganism also recovered before extubation.

Specific microbiological concordance

Specific concordance applied the same definition after exclusion of oropharyngeal flora (code 2) from both pre-extubation and POP microbiology.

Potential actionability

Potential actionability required:

  1. positive pre-extubation microbiology;
  2. specific organism-level concordance;
  3. subsequent inadequate empirical antimicrobial therapy.

This definition represents an upper-bound estimate and does not establish that the prior microbiological result was available to or used by the treating clinician.

Final interpretation

The FINAL database comprised 122 patients with postoperative pneumonia, all of whom underwent pre-extubation respiratory sampling.

Pre-extubation microbiology was positive in 81/122 (66.4%) patients.

At least one microorganism recovered before extubation was subsequently recovered at POP diagnosis in 54/81 (66.7%) positive samples.

After exclusion of non-specific oropharyngeal flora, specific organism-level concordance was observed in 33/81 (40.7%), corresponding to 27.0% of the overall cohort.

Empirical antimicrobial adequacy was evaluable in 100 patients and was inadequate in 22 (22.0%).

Among patients with specific microbiological concordance, 8 received inadequate empirical antimicrobial therapy. Thus, prior organism-specific microbiological information was potentially relevant to empirical antimicrobial selection in 8/122 (6.6%; 95% CI 2.9–12.5%) of the overall cohort.

This proportion should be interpreted as an upper-bound estimate of potential actionability, because the FINAL database establishes the date of pre-extubation sampling but does not establish the precise time at which microorganism identification and antimicrobial susceptibility results became available to the treating clinician.

Reported antimicrobial resistance was strongly associated with empirical antimicrobial inadequacy in unadjusted analysis (OR 10.02, 95% CI 3.13–36.66, P <0.001).

Overall, the FINAL data indicate that pre-extubation respiratory microbiology frequently identified microorganisms and showed subsequent microbiological overlap in a substantial subset of patients. However, organism-specific information coincided with subsequent inadequate empirical antimicrobial therapy in only a minority of the overall cohort. The clinical value of routine pre-extubation sampling therefore depends not only on microbiological concordance but also on the timely availability and actual use of prior microbiological and susceptibility information.
